title: Job
lead: Job, the man of Uz who "feared God and kept away from evil" (Job 1:1), lost his wealth, his children and his health, argued with his friends and with God, and heard the LORD answer him from the storm. Outside his own book the Bible names him twice: Ezekiel sets him beside Noah and Daniel as a model of righteousness, and James holds up his endurance.

sections.b: Ezekiel names Job with Noah and Daniel as three righteous men whose goodness could save only themselves in a land under judgment (Ezekiel 14:14, 20). Because Noah and the Daniel of Ezekiel's list (perhaps the Danel of Ugaritic legend) are ancient, non-Israelite heroes, many scholars think the story of a righteous sufferer named Job was known in Israel long before the book took its present form. James 5:11 points to "the endurance of Job" and to "the end the Lord brought about," showing that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy. Paul quotes Eliphaz's words in 1 Corinthians 3:19 and Job 41:11 in Romans 11:35. The Hebrew of Sirach 49:9 also seems to mention Job among the heroes of Israel's past.
sections.refs: Ezekiel 14:14; Ezekiel 14:20; James 5:11; 1 Corinthians 3:19; Romans 11:35; Sirach 49:9

sections.b: The Old Greek translation adds an ending that identifies Job with Jobab, a king of Edom (Genesis 36:33), and says he will rise again with those the Lord raises up (the Greek ending of Job). The Testament of Job, a Jewish work in Greek from about the first century BC or AD, retells the story as Job's farewell to his children: Job is a king who destroyed an idol's temple, Satan attacks him in revenge, and his wife Sitis sells her hair to buy him bread. The Talmud records a lively debate about when Job lived, whether he was an Israelite, and whether he lived at all (Bavli Bava Batra 15a–16b). In Islam he is the prophet Ayyub, praised in the Qur'an for patience.
